cards.text: After this, Samuel calls the people together to the LORD at Mizpah. Samuel is Israel's prophet, and he's got a message for the whole crowd. It comes straight from the LORD, the God of Israel.

cards.question: The LORD's message to Israel at Mizpah starts with a reminder. What does He say He did for them?

answers.text: Brought them up out of Egypt
Gave them a king long ago
Built them a city at Mizpah

cards.text: Then the message turns. The LORD is the God who saves them from all their troubles and afflictions, and today, He says, they have rejected Him.

cards.question: The LORD says Israel has rejected Him. Here's what they told Him: “No, set a ___ over us.”

cards.text: Samuel has Israel present themselves before the LORD by tribes and clans, so all the tribes come forward. I know this feeling, friend: YEARS in a junk drawer, holding my breath every time it opened to see who was getting picked.

cards.question: All the tribes of Israel come forward before the LORD. Which tribe is selected?
Next the tribe of Benjamin comes forward clan by clan, and the clan of Matri is selected. Then one man is selected. Who is it?

cards.text: Saul son of Kish is the pick. They go looking for him, and NOBODY can find him. So they inquire of the LORD again: “Has the man come here yet?”

cards.question: They can't find Saul anywhere. The LORD replies, “Behold, he has ___ himself among the baggage.”
They run and bring Saul out. When he stands among the people, he's a head taller than any of them.

cards.text: Then Samuel says to all the people, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” That is a BIG introduction for a man they just pulled out of the luggage.

cards.question: Samuel presents Saul as the one the LORD has chosen. All the people shout, “Long live the ___!”

cards.text: Then Samuel explains the rights of kingship to the people. The king's job description, spelled out for the whole crowd.

cards.question: Samuel explains the rights of kingship to the people, but he never writes them down.

cards.text: Samuel writes them on a scroll and lays it up before the LORD. Then he sends all the people away, each to his own home.

cards.question: Saul heads to his home in Gibeah too. Who goes with him?

cards.text: But not everybody's on board. Some worthless men say, “How can this man save us?”

cards.question: Those worthless men despise Saul and bring him no gifts. How does Saul respond?

answers.text: He calls them out in public

cards.text: Not one word from the new king. And that's where we'll leave it for now, friend, because this king's story is far from over.

findings.problem: The card says the LORD tells Israel they have rejected Him ("today, He says, they have rejected Him"). In the BSB, the LORD's quoted words end with verse 18 ("...all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’"). Verse 19 ("But today you have rejected your God, who saves you...") is Samuel speaking about God in the third person. It is not the LORD speaking. "Then the message turns" also presents verse 19 as part of the LORD's message.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The question opens with "The LORD says Israel has rejected Him." In verse 19, Samuel says this, not the LORD. The speaker of the verse is misattributed.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: No earlier card says the people asked for anything. Cards 1 to 3 only cover the Egypt reminder and the rejection. With nothing to reason from, the baker has to guess the wording of the quoted line. "Judge" is a real alternative, since Israel was led by judges.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The card calls "the rights of kingship" "the king's job description." That frames them as the king's duties. The text doesn't say what the rights of kingship contain, or whether they are the king's duties or his claims.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The right answer, "Men whose hearts God touched," is the only answer with spiritual, Bible-sounding wording. "Samuel and his servants" and "The whole tribe of Benjamin" are plain logistics. The right answer stands out by its tone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's voice is mostly flat. Only cards 5 and 11 try for a laugh. Moments built for comedy get no reaction: the whole nation selecting down to one man who has hidden in the baggage (cards 8 to 10), and the new king staying silent (card 19). Card 13's "job description" line reads as pleasant, not funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
